title: Sallowgate's Empty Boxes
passage:
The bat boxes on the north gable of the Sallowgate laundry have been up for eleven years. Not one of them has ever held a bat. They are handsome objects, cast in a pale aggregate that matches the render and set flush with the wall, each with a rough landing strip beneath a slot two fingers wide, and they went up under a condition of the planning consent that turned the laundry into flats. Four streets away, on a school converted the same year, a row of boxes in the same position on the same kind of gable fills most summers. For a long time nobody at the borough could say what separated the two.

Emrys Talbourne has surveyed roosts for Drimmond council since the conversions began, and he spent three summers logging temperatures rather than counting animals. The colonies displaced by the work had mostly been living in roof voids — the shallow, dusty gap between the slates and the boarding beneath them, running the length of a ridge. A void of that kind is not one habitat but a shifting range of them. Slate heats quickly. By four in the afternoon the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees while the eaves end, shaded and open to the air, sits ten or twelve degrees below it, and by dawn the whole void has given its heat back. Talbourne's loggers show the animals working through that gradient: high and deep in the warm hours, when the young grow fastest, out towards the cooler eaves at night. "I would not say they are choosing a temperature," he told me. "I would say that where the choice is missing, they do not stay long."

Not everyone in the borough reads the record that way. Beatrix Oyelaran, Drimmond's building conservation officer, thinks the temperature account has been asked to carry more than it can. Her objection is documentary, and it is about timing. She went back through the consent files and found that most of the boxes that failed had been opened in June or July, when the local colonies were long settled for the season and had no reason to prospect for anywhere new. Among the earliest boxes, those fitted between September and February were taken up about three times as often as the summer ones. "You can hang the finest box in the county in the middle of July," she said, "and it will stand empty, and that will have nothing to do with what it is made of." On the early boxes she was plainly right, and Talbourne says so.

What he did next was hold the timing constant. Across two autumns twenty-four boxes went up on nine buildings, all fitted out of season and all logged: twelve cut from thick untreated timber, twelve cast in the same aggregate as the laundry's. The timber boxes moved about eleven degrees between afternoon and dawn, and nine of the twelve were occupied within two summers. The cast boxes held to three degrees or less, and two were used. Both of those two sat on a chimney breast whose flue still carried warm air up from the block's boiler, and the loggers inside them recorded a swing much like the timber's; cast boxes on two other south-facing walls, with nothing behind them but insulation, stayed empty. One of the three timber boxes that stayed empty hangs over a yard lit all night; Talbourne suspects the lighting and has not tested it. The school's row, he adds, is boarded timber, and it swings twelve degrees. Oyelaran accepts the second series and still holds that timing explains more of the whole record than he allows.

Drimmond's guidance was rewritten last winter. It names a material, caps the wall thickness of a box, and requires that new ones be fitted between September and the end of February, though the fire officer has asked for the timber clause to be looked at again. Nothing in it reaches the boxes already on walls, and nobody has proposed taking those down. The row on the laundry's north gable is still there, still flush, still pale against the render. No one has had a ladder up to it since March.
— Perrin Hadleigh

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 1, first local item in passage order. WHY-KEY (C): paragraph 1 states that 'Four streets away, on a school converted the same year, a row of boxes in the same position on the same kind of gable fills most summers.' C paraphrases both halves — the hedged occupancy ('in most summers') and the matched position and date — without lifting a distinctive run. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = quantifier_upgrade (the engineered dominant ELF trap) — absolutises the planted hedge 'fills most summers' into 'full every single summer'; tempting because a skimmer remembers only that the school's row works. B = outside_knowledge — imports a plausible explanation (autumn fitting versus a July fitting at the laundry) that the passage never states about either row; the June/July finding in paragraph 3 concerns 'most of the boxes that failed' across the borough, not this pair, and the text says 'For a long time nobody at the borough could say what separated the two'. D = wrong_location — the 'three summers' of logging belong to Talbourne's own survey work in paragraph 2 ('he spent three summers logging temperatures rather than counting animals'), not to the school's row, and no condition on conversions is said to follow from it.

questions.prompt: What are we told about the roof voids the displaced colonies had been using?

options.text: The whole of a void stayed close to thirty degrees from the middle of the afternoon until first light.
Heat rising from the rooms below kept the space above the boarding warmer than the air outside at night.
They were narrow enough that a colony had to settle near the ridge and stay there for the whole season.
One end of a void was far warmer than the other, and the animals moved between the two.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-001 (direct detail retrieval), anchored in paragraph 2, local order. STEM-LAW: the stem names the voids but entails nothing about what they were like, so all four options are open on form. WHY-KEY (D): paragraph 2 reports that 'the space near the ridge can stand close to thirty degrees while the eaves end, shaded and open to the air, sits ten or twelve degrees below it', and that 'Talbourne's loggers show the animals working through that gradient: high and deep in the warm hours, when the young grow fastest, out towards the cooler eaves at night.' D states exactly that spatial difference plus the movement, in different words. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = scope_error on a real figure — takes the thirty degrees measured only at the ridge end and spreads it over 'the whole of a void', and over the night as well, which the same sentence contradicts ('by dawn the whole void has given its heat back'). B = outside_knowledge — a genuinely plausible building-physics claim (warmth from the rooms below) that the passage never makes; the text attributes the heat to the slate ('Slate heats quickly'). C = quantifier_upgrade / contradicted — turns the void into a single fixed spot and denies the movement the loggers recorded; tempting because the ridge end is named first and is the warmest.

questions.prompt: What does the passage suggest about the two cast boxes that were occupied?

options.text: The range of temperature inside them was supplied by the warm flue behind, not by the boxes.
They were the only cast boxes in the trial that had been fitted on a south-facing wall.
Cast boxes work as well as timber ones provided they are hung high on a sunny wall.
Their aggregate had been mixed thinner than the laundry's, so it gave up its heat more quickly.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-002 (inference / implication), one logical inch beyond paragraph 4. WHY-KEY (A): paragraph 4 reports that 'The cast boxes held to three degrees or less, and two were used. Both of those two sat on a chimney breast whose flue still carried warm air up from the block's boiler, and the loggers inside them recorded a swing much like the timber's.' Cast material by itself held three degrees or less; these two swung like timber; the one thing behind them that the others lacked was a live flue. The inference is that the range was supplied by the building, not by the box — exactly what A says. WHY-DISTRACTORS: B = too_literal / contradicted — fastens on aspect rather than the flue, and the same sentence records 'cast boxes on two other south-facing walls, with nothing behind them but insulation, stayed empty', so these two were not the only south-facing cast boxes. C = too_far — a two-step leap into a general recommendation about how cast boxes should be hung; the passage reports two boxes on one heated breast, not a rule for sunny walls. D = outside_knowledge — invents a difference in the mix that the text never mentions; the passage says the trial boxes were 'cast in the same aggregate as the laundry's'.

questions.prompt: What is the writer's attitude to Oyelaran's objection?

options.text: Convinced: the writer holds with her that what a box is made of hardly matters at all.
Sceptical: the writer grants the objection some force but thinks her file search far too small.
Accepting as far as it goes: right about the earliest boxes, but not about the later series.
Dismissive: the writer treats it as a procedural complaint that the temperature record has already answered.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-005 (stance / tone / attitude); the challenger here is partly right, so the item turns on how far the writer goes with her. Hedge-balanced by design: A, B and C are all qualified in form and only D is absolute, so 'pick the hedged option' does not score the item. WHY-KEY (C): the writer endorses the timing point in plain words — 'On the early boxes she was plainly right, and Talbourne says so' — but then reports the second series, in which 'What he did next was hold the timing constant' and all twenty-four boxes were 'fitted out of season', and lets the timber/cast split stand as a result the timing objection does not reach; Oyelaran's continuing claim that 'timing explains more of the whole record than he allows' is reported as her position, not endorsed. C names precisely that bounded acceptance. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = role_or_attribution_swap (the TYPE-005 signature) — hands the writer Oyelaran's own quoted claim that an empty box 'will have nothing to do with what it is made of'; tempting because hers is the most forceful line in the text, and A is softened ('hardly matters') so that it does not read as an obvious overstatement. B = polarity error in the qualified register — the writer never questions her file search and never calls the sample small; the text concedes the point outright. D = polarity overshoot — turns a granted objection into a complaint brushed aside, which 'she was plainly right' contradicts.

questions.prompt: What is this text mainly about?

options.text: The conditions that planning authorities attach to the conversion of old buildings into housing.
Why some purpose-built replacement roosts are taken up by bats while others stand empty.
Talbourne's decision to give up counting animals altogether and record temperatures in their place.
A disagreement between two council officers over how much of a converted building should be kept.

questions.rationale: Family ELF-TYPE-004 (main idea / whole-text focus), edge position 5. WHY-KEY (B): the passage opens on a matched pair — the laundry's boxes where 'Not one of them has ever held a bat' beside a school row that 'fills most summers' — states that 'For a long time nobody at the borough could say what separated the two', works through the void measurements, the timing objection and the twenty-four-box series, and ends with a rewritten guidance and one row still empty. The question the whole text pursues is which replacement boxes get used and which do not; B states that without claiming the answer is settled. WHY-DISTRACTORS: A = scope_error — planning conditions are the frame in which the boxes exist ('a condition of the planning consent that turned the laundry into flats') and the closing paragraph does report a rewritten guidance, but the text argues nothing about planning practice in general. C = detail-as-main, distorted — Talbourne did spend 'three summers logging temperatures rather than counting animals', but 'give up counting animals altogether' overstates a method choice within one survey, and a method is not the text's subject. D = surface_word_match — Talbourne and Oyelaran do disagree, yet about why boxes fail, not about how much original fabric a conversion should keep; the phrase borrows her job title ('building conservation officer') for a dispute the text never stages.
